description: A large theropod dinosaur that lived in what is now western North America, among the last non-avian dinosaurs before the end-Cretaceous extinction.
A large horned dinosaur known for its distinctive three-horned skull and bony frill, one of the last ceratopsians before the K-Pg extinction.
A small, feathered, bipedal dromaeosaurid dinosaur from Mongolia, roughly turkey-sized in real life, closely related to birds.
An armored dinosaur recognized for the row of large plates along its back and spikes on its tail.
A giant long-necked sauropod with disproportionately long forelimbs, among the tallest known dinosaurs.
A very large theropod with a distinctive sail-like structure on its back, adapted for a semi-aquatic, fish-eating lifestyle in North Africa.
A heavily armored dinosaur with a large bony club at the end of its tail, used for defense.
A duck-billed dinosaur known for its long, curved cranial crest, likely used for vocalization and display.
A cold-adapted elephant relative covered in long fur, common across the mammoth steppe of Eurasia and North America until roughly 4,000 years ago.
A large predatory cat known for its extremely long, blade-like upper canine teeth, found widely in the Americas.
One of the largest known land mammals of its time, an elephant-sized ground-dwelling sloth from South America.
A large flightless bird endemic to Mauritius, driven to extinction within decades of sustained human contact.
A large crested pterosaur with a wingspan of over 6 meters, not a dinosaur but a separate group of flying reptiles.
One of the largest known flying animals of all time, an azhdarchid pterosaur with an estimated wingspan of around 10-11 meters.
A transitional feathered dinosaur/early bird from Germany, often cited as one of the key fossils linking dinosaurs and modern birds.
A huge marine lizard, not a dinosaur, that was an apex predator of the Late Cretaceous seas.
A dolphin-shaped marine reptile, an early and well-studied example of convergent evolution with fish and dolphins.
A long-necked marine reptile with four large flippers, historically the type genus for all plesiosaurs.
An enormous extinct shark, among the largest predatory fish to have ever lived, known mostly from fossil teeth.
The largest living land animal, found across sub-Saharan Africa, threatened by poaching and habitat loss.
A tiger subspecies found mainly in India and Bangladesh, the most numerous tiger population, still under significant conservation pressure.
A bear native to south-central China with a diet consisting almost entirely of bamboo, a global conservation icon.
A highly social canid and the ancestor of the domestic dog, historically the most widely distributed land mammal predator.
North America's largest land mammal, reduced from tens of millions to near-extinction in the 1800s before conservation efforts restored wild herds.
The largest living lizard species, found only on a handful of Indonesian islands.
The largest animal known to have ever existed, larger than any dinosaur, found in oceans worldwide.
A large predatory shark found in coastal and offshore waters worldwide, the largest known predatory fish.
A large sea turtle found in tropical and subtropical oceans, named for the greenish color of its fat.
A widely studied, highly intelligent marine mammal found in temperate and tropical waters worldwide.
The largest living reptile, found in coastal wetlands and rivers across South and Southeast Asia and northern Australia.
The tallest and heaviest of all living penguin species, native to Antarctica and dependent on sea ice for breeding.
A large bird of prey native to North America and the national bird of the United States, recovered from near-extinction after DDT was banned.
A widespread bird of prey renowned as the fastest animal on Earth, capable of diving at over 300 km/h (190 mph).
A migratory butterfly famous for its multi-generational annual migration between North America and central Mexico.
A large bipedal predatory theropod, one of the most common large carnivores of the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation.
A very long, whip-tailed sauropod, one of the longest dinosaurs known from a fairly complete skeleton.
A massive, long-necked sauropod formerly confused with Brontosaurus, known for its thick, heavily built neck.
A large herbivorous ornithopod and one of the first dinosaurs ever formally named, in 1825.
A mid-sized, sickle-clawed dromaeosaurid whose discovery in the 1960s helped spark the idea that dinosaurs were active, bird-like animals.
A South American theropod notable for the pair of thick horns above its eyes and its unusually small forelimbs.
A large, herbivorous theropod best known for its enormous claws, among the longest of any known animal.
A small, chicken-sized theropod, one of the smallest known non-avian dinosaurs.
An early, crested theropod from Arizona, one of the largest land animals of its time.
A fish-eating spinosaurid with a long, crocodile-like snout, discovered in England in the 1980s.
A large, fast, ostrich-like theropod from Mongolia with a toothless beak.
A dome-headed herbivorous dinosaur, thought to have used its thick skull roof in head-butting or flank-butting behavior.
A large duck-billed dinosaur known from numerous well-preserved skeletons, including rare fossilized skin impressions.
A small, slender, early theropod known from a mass death assemblage in New Mexico, among the earliest well-known dinosaurs.
A small, primitive dinosaur from Argentina, considered one of the earliest known dinosaurs.
A huge South American theropod, among the largest terrestrial predators known, rivaling Tyrannosaurus in size.
A horned dinosaur with a distinctive frill ringed by long spikes, related to Triceratops.
A giant, humpbacked ornithomimosaur known for its enormous arms, long a mystery until more complete fossils were found in 2014.
A cold-adapted, thickly furred rhinoceros that lived across Ice Age Eurasia alongside woolly mammoths.
A car-sized, heavily armored relative of modern armadillos, native to South America.
An enormous deer, not actually restricted to Ireland, famous for having the largest antlers of any known deer species.
A large Ice Age bear known from thousands of skeletons found in European caves.
A large, flightless, predatory bird with a massive hooked beak, part of a South American lineage of apex-predator birds.
A tusked, elephant-like mammal distinct from mammoths, adapted to browsing in forested Ice Age North America.
One of the largest bears known to have existed, a long-legged Ice Age predator of North America.
An early pterosaur with a large, puffin-like head and long tail, discovered by Mary Anning in England.
A long-tailed pterosaur with needle-like teeth, known from exceptionally preserved fossils in Germany.
The first pterosaur ever scientifically described, giving rise to the popular but technically informal term 'pterodactyl'.
A tern-like, toothed seabird, one of the closest known relatives to modern birds among Mesozoic species.
A large, short-necked marine reptile (pliosaur) with a powerful bite, an apex predator of Jurassic seas.
A plesiosaur with an extraordinarily long neck made up of more than 70 vertebrae.
A huge ichthyosaur, among the largest marine reptiles known, with fossils concentrated in Nevada.
An early, fully aquatic whale with an elongated, serpentine body, despite its name meaning 'king lizard'.
A heavily armored, giant predatory fish with self-sharpening bony jaw plates instead of teeth.
A large, flightless, foot-propelled diving bird from the Late Cretaceous seas of North America.
A large, fanged predatory bony fish, one of the largest of its kind, famous for fossils preserved with swallowed prey inside.
A shark-like cartilaginous fish famous for its bizarre spiral 'tooth whorl', the arrangement of which puzzled scientists for decades.
A large cat adapted to the mountains of Central and South Asia, prized for its thick spotted coat.
The fastest land animal, capable of short bursts over 100 km/h, found across parts of Africa and Iran.
The tallest living land animal, native to the savannas of sub-Saharan Africa.
A small, arboreal mammal native to the eastern Himalayas, not closely related to the giant panda despite the shared name.
A great ape native to the island of Borneo, one of humanity's closest living relatives, threatened by deforestation.
A gorilla subspecies found in the mountain forests of the Virunga volcanoes region of central Africa.
A highly intelligent great ape and one of the two closest living relatives to humans, native to equatorial Africa.
A browsing African rhinoceros species that has suffered severe population declines due to poaching for its horn.
The largest living rhinoceros species, a grazing grassland species native to southern and central Africa.
A large Arctic bear that hunts seals from sea ice, considered especially vulnerable to climate change.
A large, social big cat found in sub-Saharan Africa, one of the most recognizable predators in the world.
The largest cat native to the Americas, known for its powerful bite and preference for dense forest near water.
A stocky, powerful member of the weasel family found in northern boreal and Arctic regions.
A small fox adapted to extreme cold, with a thick coat that changes color with the seasons.
The most widely distributed wild carnivore in the world, found across the Northern Hemisphere and introduced to Australia.
An adaptable North American canid whose range has expanded significantly alongside human development.
An Australian marsupial that feeds almost exclusively on eucalyptus leaves.
The largest living marsupial, native to the arid interior of Australia.
A small but notoriously fearless mustelid found across Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia.
A nocturnal, burrowing African mammal that feeds on ants and termites, the only living species in its taxonomic order.
A small, highly social mongoose relative native to southern Africa's arid regions, known for its sentry behavior.
The largest living bird, flightless but capable of running at over 70 km/h, native to Africa.
The largest member of the dolphin family and an apex ocean predator found in every ocean on Earth.
A large baleen whale famous for its complex songs and acrobatic breaching, found in oceans worldwide.
The largest living ray species, a filter feeder found in warm, temperate, and tropical waters worldwide.
The largest living fish species, a slow-moving filter feeder despite its enormous size.
The largest hammerhead shark species, named for its distinctively wide, flattened head.
The largest living sea turtle, with a distinctive leathery shell instead of a hard, bony carapace.
A small, all-white Arctic and sub-Arctic whale known for its expressive face and wide vocal repertoire.
An Arctic whale whose males grow a long, spiraled tusk, actually an elongated tooth.
A large African crocodile found in rivers, lakes, and wetlands, one of the continent's most formidable predators.
A large reptile native to the southeastern United States, a notable conservation success story after near-extinction in the 20th century.
One of the largest and most widespread birds of prey in the Northern Hemisphere.
A large, powerful owl found throughout the Americas, recognizable by its prominent ear tufts.
A tiny migratory hummingbird found in eastern North America, capable of flying nonstop across the Gulf of Mexico.
A seabird famous for the longest known migration of any animal, traveling between Arctic and Antarctic regions each year.
One of the largest flying birds in the world by wingspan, native to the Andes mountains of South America.
A seabird with the largest wingspan of any living bird, able to glide for hours over the Southern Ocean without flapping.
The most widespread flamingo species, known for its pink plumage derived from carotenoid pigments in its diet.
A highly social, eusocial insect central to pollination of crops and wild plants worldwide.
